questions.question: What are wrapper classes in Java and why do they exist?
questions.title: Wrapper Classes
questions.direct_answer: Wrapper classes like Integer, Double, Boolean, Character, Long, Float, Byte, and Short convert Java's eight primitive types into objects. They exist because Java collections and generics require objects—primitives can't be stored in ArrayList or HashMap. They also provide utility methods for parsing and conversion.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of Java's dual type system (primitives vs objects) and why the language needs both
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forgetting that char maps to Character and int maps to Integer (not Int), or thinking primitives can be used directly in generics like List<int>
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that all numeric wrappers extend the abstract Number class, and mention autoboxing/unboxing introduced in Java 5 to simplify conversions

sections.title: Why Java Has Two Type Systems
sections.content: Java has eight **primitive types** (int, double, boolean, char, long, float, byte, short) that store raw values directly in memory for performance. But the entire Collections Framework and generics require **objects**—you can't create an ArrayList<int>. **Wrapper classes** solve this by wrapping each primitive in an object shell. For example, Integer wraps int, Double wraps double, and Character wraps char. Beyond enabling collections, wrappers provide **utility methods** like Integer.parseInt() to convert strings to numbers, and constants like Integer.MAX_VALUE. The **Number** abstract class sits at the top of the numeric wrapper hierarchy, allowing polymorphic code that accepts any numeric type. Think of wrappers as gift boxes: the primitive is the gift, the wrapper is the box that lets you ship it through Java's object-based APIs.

sections.title: Using Wrapper Classes in Collections and Parsing
Key Points
content: **Eight wrappers**: Integer, Double, Boolean, Character, Long, Float, Byte, Short—one per primitive type
**Collections requirement**: generics like List<T> and Map<K,V> can only hold objects, never primitives like int or double
**Autoboxing/unboxing**: Java automatically converts between primitives and wrappers since Java 5, making code cleaner
**Number hierarchy**: Integer, Double, Long, Float, Byte, Short all extend the abstract Number class, enabling polymorphic numeric operations
**Utility methods**: wrappers provide parsing (parseInt), conversion (intValue), comparison (compare), and constants (MAX_VALUE, MIN_VALUE)
**Immutability**: all wrapper objects are immutable—you can't change an Integer's value after creation
**null capability**: wrapper objects can be null (unlike primitives), useful for representing missing or optional values

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Wrapper classes convert Java's eight primitive types into objects. Java has primitives like int, double, and boolean for speed, but collections and generics can only work with objects. You can't make a List of int, but you can make a List of Integer. That's the main reason wrappers exist. Each primitive has a matching wrapper: int becomes Integer, double becomes Double, char becomes Character, and so on. All the numeric wrappers like Integer and Double extend an abstract class called Number, which gives you conversion methods like intValue and doubleValue. Wrappers also give you utility methods. For example, Integer has parseInt to convert strings to numbers, and constants like MAX_VALUE. Since Java 5, autoboxing handles the conversion automatically—when you add an int to a List of Integer, Java wraps it for you. One thing to watch: wrapper objects can be null, which primitives can't be. That's useful for database fields or optional values, but it means you can get NullPointerException if you're not careful when unboxing.

questions.question: What is the difference between Integer.parseInt() and Integer.valueOf()?
questions.title: parseInt() vs valueOf()
questions.direct_answer: Integer.parseInt() returns a primitive int by parsing a string. Integer.valueOf() returns an Integer object, and it uses an internal cache for values between -128 and 127, returning the same object instance for those values to save memory.

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge of the Integer cache and when to use primitive returns versus object returns
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using parseInt when you need to add the result to a collection (requiring autoboxing), or comparing cached Integer objects with == and not understanding why it works for small numbers but fails for large ones
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the Integer cache range (-128 to 127) and demonstrate that valueOf is more efficient than new Integer() because of caching

sections.title: Parsing Strings to Integers: Primitive vs Object
sections.content: Both methods convert a string like "123" into a number, but they return different types. **Integer.parseInt(String s)** returns a primitive int—just the raw number value. **Integer.valueOf(String s)** returns an Integer object wrapping that value. The key difference is the **Integer cache**: Java pre-creates Integer objects for values -128 to 127 and reuses them. When you call valueOf with "100", you get a cached object. When you call it with "1000", Java creates a new object. This caching saves memory and improves performance for common small numbers. The parseInt method has no cache because it returns a primitive, which doesn't occupy heap memory. Choose parseInt when you need a primitive for calculations, and valueOf when you need an object for collections or APIs expecting Integer.

rows: Fast for cached range, slower otherwise

sections.title: When to Use Each Method
sections.content: Use **parseInt()** when you're doing math or logic with the result—like calculating totals, comparing values, or indexing arrays. It returns a primitive int, which is faster and uses no heap memory. Use **valueOf()** when you need to store the result in a collection like List<Integer> or Map<String, Integer>, or when working with Optional<Integer>. It's also better when the value might be absent (null). If you're parsing user input in a loop and just summing numbers, parseInt is the right choice. If you're building a cache of parsed values or returning from a method that needs to indicate "no value" with null, use valueOf. Remember that valueOf is equivalent to Integer.parseInt() followed by autoboxing, but it's more efficient because of the cache for small numbers.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Return type difference**: parseInt returns primitive int, valueOf returns Integer object
**Integer cache**: valueOf reuses the same object instances for values from -128 to 127, saving memory
**Equality trap**: Integer objects from valueOf compare with == correctly in the cached range, but fail outside it—always use equals()
**Autoboxing**: calling parseInt and storing in an Integer variable triggers autoboxing, which is less efficient than valueOf
**NumberFormatException**: both methods throw this unchecked exception if the string isn't a valid number
**Radix support**: both accept a second parameter for parsing in different bases like binary (2) or hexadecimal (16)
**Performance**: parseInt is marginally faster since it avoids object creation, but the difference is negligible in most applications

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The main difference is what they return. parseInt returns a primitive int, while valueOf returns an Integer object. If you're doing math with the result, use parseInt—it's faster because there's no object creation. If you're storing the result in a collection like a List of Integer, use valueOf because collections need objects. There's another important detail: valueOf uses something called the Integer cache. Java pre-creates Integer objects for numbers from negative 128 to positive 127, and valueOf reuses those objects. So if you parse "50" twice with valueOf, you get the exact same object both times. You can even compare them with double-equals and it returns true. But if you parse "500" twice, you get two different objects, and double-equals returns false. That's why you should always use equals to compare Integer objects, not double-equals. A common mistake is using parseInt when you're about to add the result to an ArrayList. That causes autoboxing, which is less efficient than just calling valueOf directly. Both methods throw NumberFormatException if the string isn't a valid number, so you usually wrap them in try-catch.

questions.question: What are Integer.MAX_VALUE and Integer.MIN_VALUE and where are they used?
questions.title: Integer Bounds
questions.direct_answer: Integer.MAX_VALUE is 2,147,483,647 (2 to the power of 31 minus 1), and Integer.MIN_VALUE is negative 2,147,483,648 (negative 2 to the power of 31). They're used as initial values when finding maximum or minimum in arrays, and for detecting integer overflow in calculations.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of integer bounds and practical algorithm patterns like finding max/min
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Hardcoding large numbers like 999999999 instead of using MAX_VALUE, or not understanding that MAX_VALUE plus one wraps around to MIN_VALUE due to overflow
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Demonstrate overflow behavior by showing that Integer.MAX_VALUE plus one equals Integer.MIN_VALUE, and explain why this matters in production code

sections.title: Integer Bounds and Their Practical Uses
sections.content: Java's **int** type is a 32-bit signed integer, meaning it can represent 2 to the power of 32 different values, split between positive and negative. **Integer.MAX_VALUE** (2,147,483,647) is the largest positive int, and **Integer.MIN_VALUE** (negative 2,147,483,648) is the smallest. These constants are essential in **algorithms**: when finding the maximum element in an array, you initialize your result to MIN_VALUE so any real element is larger. Similarly, initialize to MAX_VALUE when finding a minimum. They're also critical for **overflow detection**—if you add 1 to MAX_VALUE, it wraps around to MIN_VALUE instead of throwing an exception. In production, this silent overflow causes bugs like negative bank balances or corrupted timestamps. The constants make your code readable and portable—if Java's int size ever changed (unlikely), your code would still work. Think of them as the walls of a circular track: run past the finish line and you're back at the start.

sections.title: Using MAX_VALUE and MIN_VALUE in Algorithms
Key Points
content: **MAX_VALUE is 2^31 - 1**: equals 2,147,483,647, the largest positive int Java can represent in 32 bits
**MIN_VALUE is -2^31**: equals negative 2,147,483,648, not positive—this is the most negative int
**Algorithm initialization**: use MIN_VALUE to initialize max-finding, MAX_VALUE for min-finding so first comparison succeeds
**Overflow wraps silently**: adding 1 to MAX_VALUE produces MIN_VALUE with no exception—Java doesn't signal integer overflow
**Math.addExact alternative**: Java 8 added Math.addExact(int, int) which throws ArithmeticException on overflow instead of wrapping
**Comparison with long bounds**: if your values might exceed int range, use Long.MAX_VALUE (9,223,372,036,854,775,807) instead
**Sentinel values**: MAX_VALUE and MIN_VALUE are often used as sentinel values meaning "infinity" or "undefined" in graph algorithms

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Integer.MAX_VALUE is about 2.1 billion—specifically, it's 2 to the power of 31 minus 1, which is 2,147,483,647. Integer.MIN_VALUE is negative 2 to the power of 31, about negative 2.1 billion. These represent the bounds of a 32-bit signed integer. They're super useful in coding problems. When you're finding the maximum element in an array, you initialize your max variable to Integer.MIN_VALUE. That way, the first element you check will definitely be larger. Same thing in reverse: initialize to MAX_VALUE when finding a minimum. Here's the tricky part: if you add 1 to MAX_VALUE, it doesn't throw an error. It wraps around to MIN_VALUE because of how binary math works. This is called integer overflow, and it causes real bugs in production—like when a game's score goes negative after hitting a milestone. A common mistake freshers make is hardcoding something like 999999999 as a starting value instead of using Integer.MIN_VALUE. That's fragile because an array element could actually be bigger than your hardcoded number. If you need to detect overflow before it happens, you can check if your value is greater than MAX_VALUE minus whatever you're adding. Or use Math.addExact, which throws an exception instead of wrapping.

questions.question: What useful methods does the Character class provide for string processing?
questions.title: Character Class Methods
questions.direct_answer: The Character class provides isDigit(), isLetter(), isUpperCase(), isLowerCase(), isWhitespace(), toUpperCase(), toLowerCase() for validation and transformation, plus getNumericValue() to convert digit characters like '7' to the integer 7.

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge of the Character API for implementing string validation and parsing logic
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Writing manual checks like c greater-than-or-equal '0' and c less-than-or-equal '9' instead of using Character.isDigit, or forgetting that Character methods work with Unicode, not just ASCII
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show Character.getNumericValue for converting '5' to 5, and explain that Character methods handle international characters correctly unlike manual ASCII range checks

sections.title: Character API for String Processing
sections.content: The **Character class** wraps the primitive char and provides static utility methods essential for processing strings character-by-character. Methods like **isDigit(char c)** and **isLetter(char c)** classify characters, answering questions like "is this a number?" or "is this alphabetic?". **isUpperCase()** and **isLowerCase()** check case, while **toUpperCase()** and **toLowerCase()** transform characters. **isWhitespace()** detects spaces, tabs, and newlines—critical for parsing user input. Unlike manual checks like c >= '0' && c <= '9', these methods handle **Unicode** correctly, recognizing digits and letters from non-English languages. **Character.getNumericValue(char c)** is particularly powerful: it converts a digit character like '7' into the integer 7, cleaner than subtracting '0'. These methods eliminate error-prone manual range checks and make your string validation code readable and internationalization-friendly. Think of Character as your validation toolkit: instead of building logic from scratch, reach for the right tool.

sections.title: Validating and Parsing Strings with Character Methods
Key Points
content: **isDigit(char c)**: returns true for '0' through '9' and Unicode digits from other languages—cleaner than manual c >= '0' && c <= '9'
**isLetter(char c)**: checks if character is alphabetic, including accented letters and non-English alphabets
**isUpperCase/isLowerCase**: checks character case, useful for password validation and format checking
**toUpperCase/toLowerCase**: converts case of a single character—String has similar methods for entire strings
**isWhitespace(char c)**: matches space, tab, newline, and other whitespace—more comprehensive than checking == ' '
**getNumericValue(char c)**: converts digit character '7' to integer 7, avoiding the c minus '0' trick
**Unicode support**: all Character methods correctly handle international characters, making your code globally compatible

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The Character class gives you utility methods for working with individual characters in strings. The most common ones are isDigit, isLetter, isUpperCase, isLowerCase, and isWhitespace. If you're validating user input, like checking if a username contains only letters and numbers, you'd loop through the string and call Character.isDigit and Character.isLetter on each character. That's way cleaner than manually checking if c is greater than or equal to '0' and less than or equal to '9'. There's also toUpperCase and toLowerCase for converting case. One really useful method is getNumericValue. If you have the character '5' and need the integer 5, just call Character.getNumericValue. That's more readable than subtracting the character '0'. A big advantage of these methods is Unicode support. They correctly recognize digits and letters from languages like Arabic or Chinese, while manual checks only work for English ASCII. I've used these a lot in coding problems—like checking if a string is alphanumeric, or parsing a string where digits need special handling. The isWhitespace method is handy too because it catches tabs and newlines, not just spaces.

questions.question: What is the Number class hierarchy in Java?
questions.title: Number Class Hierarchy
questions.direct_answer: Number is an abstract class that Integer, Long, Double, Float, Byte, and Short extend. It also includes BigDecimal and BigInteger. It defines abstract methods like intValue() and doubleValue() that convert any numeric type to a primitive, enabling polymorphic numeric operations.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of Java's class hierarchy and how wrapper classes relate through inheritance
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking only the six basic wrappers extend Number, forgetting BigDecimal and BigInteger are also subclasses
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that Number enables writing generic numeric methods accepting any wrapper type, like void calculate(Number n), and mention the conversion methods it provides

sections.title: The Number Class Hierarchy
sections.content: **Number** is an abstract class in java.lang that sits at the top of the numeric type hierarchy. Six primitive wrappers extend it: **Integer, Long, Double, Float, Byte, and Short**. Additionally, **BigDecimal** (for arbitrary-precision decimals) and **BigInteger** (for arbitrarily large whole numbers) also extend Number. The class defines six abstract methods—**intValue(), longValue(), doubleValue(), floatValue(), byteValue(), shortValue()**—that every subclass must implement. These methods convert the wrapped number to any primitive numeric type, handling the conversion automatically. This hierarchy enables **polymorphism**: you can write a method accepting Number and pass any numeric type. For example, a method void processMetric(Number value) works with Integer sales, Double revenue, or BigDecimal profit. Number provides type flexibility without requiring overloaded methods for every numeric type. Think of Number as a contract: "I'm some kind of number, and I can tell you my value as an int, double, or any other numeric type."

sections.title: Using Number for Polymorphic Numeric Code
Key Points
content: **Abstract class**: Number is abstract, meaning you can't instantiate it—only its concrete subclasses
**Six wrapper subclasses**: Integer, Long, Double, Float, Byte, Short all extend Number and represent primitive types
**Big number classes**: BigDecimal and BigInteger also extend Number for arbitrary-precision calculations
**Conversion methods**: Number defines intValue, doubleValue, longValue, floatValue, byteValue, shortValue for type conversion
**Polymorphic parameters**: methods can accept Number to work with any numeric type, avoiding method overloading
**Precision loss**: calling intValue on a Double like 3.7 truncates to 3, not rounding—conversion can lose information
**Collections flexibility**: List<Number> can hold any mix of Integer, Double, BigDecimal in the same collection

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Number is an abstract class that all the numeric wrapper classes extend. The six basic wrappers—Integer, Long, Double, Float, Byte, and Short—are all subclasses of Number. What people sometimes forget is that BigDecimal and BigInteger also extend Number. Those are the classes you use when you need really precise decimal math or really huge integers that don't fit in a long. The Number class defines six abstract methods: intValue, longValue, doubleValue, floatValue, byteValue, and shortValue. Every subclass implements these to convert its value to any primitive numeric type. So you can take an Integer and call doubleValue on it, and Java handles the conversion. The main benefit is polymorphism. You can write a method that takes a Number parameter, and it'll accept any numeric type—Integer, Double, BigDecimal, whatever. That's cleaner than writing separate overloaded methods for each type. For example, if you're building a calculator or processing financial data, you can work with Number and not care whether the caller passes an Integer or a BigDecimal. One thing to watch: when you call intValue on a Double like 3.7, it truncates to 3. It doesn't round, so you might lose precision.
